image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Grouped horizontal bar chart.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- The visualization uses **small multiples / faceting by response category**.  
- There are four side-by-side panels: **Education**, **Hard work**, **Family wealth or connections**, and **All, none or other**.  
- Each panel contains horizontal bars for the same set of countries.  
- No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis (rows of horizontal bars) |
| Response share / percentage of 15–24-year-olds | Quantitative | Bar length / position along x-axis |
| Most important factor in determining success (Education, Hard work, Family wealth or connections, All/none/other) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Country wealth order (richest to poorest, per note) | Ordinal | Vertical ordering of countries on the y-axis |

The US also has a fairly high percentage of people who believe hard work is an important factor in determining success, but low percentage that education is an important factor. I wonder how this affects US citizen's motivation to attend college and get a higher education versus starting a career early on and working hard to gain success. Most of the other countries believe that education is a much more important factor of success than countries such as the US, Japan, and Kenya. Finally, I wonder how the US's strong belief that family wealth and connections play a role in success affect citizen's motivation to work hard. My title for this graph would be "What do different countries believe is the key to success?"

But in a country like India, for example, where there are a lot more impoverished people, they mostly viewed education as the single determining factor in establishing success. A title could be "success in different countries"

The first thing I noticed is the comparison between the US and the other countries. It is clear that the US thinks family wealth and connections are most important when determining success. However, other countries like Brazil, Peru and Argentina believe that education is the most important. This makes me wonder why the young people in the US think this way. Also what the difference is between what the US and other countries are teaching their young ones about success. This obviously affects my community because I live in the US, and this gives insight to how my generation views success and how things in the country are being run might be affecting people's perception of success.

The main thing I noticed was how a majority of young people think the most important factor in determining success in education and hard work. I also noticed some countries that had very different results. For example, while many young people believe hard work is important, they also think wealth/connections are very important while Indonesia thinks that hard work is very important and wealth/connections are the least important. This makes me wonder what aspects of each country influence these decisions. For example, quality of education, availability of higher education, etc. It also makes me wonder how much culture may influence the decision of young people. This relates to me because I fall within the age group that answered this graph's question. 

Possible catchy headline: "The Recipe to Success"

So Called Success?
There is definitely a clear trend in certain countries in determining the factors for success.  It is interesting to see these trends because I feel as though American society stereotypes peoples from these countries in a way that coincidently corresponds with their ideas of success.  For example, for the most part, American's believe that success comes from mostly connections given the common phrase "it's all about who you know".  On the other hand, American's stereotype certain races, Asians for example, based on their intelligence.  This intelligence, given what the country determines success as, is rooted upon hard work and education. I wonder since this is a collection of younger generational responses that these ideals are engraved because of social norms within the society or if it's as natural as American's assume these attributes to be.

It raises the question of what do these children constitute as hard work since it seems to not be hard work in school. However, in Spanish-speaking countries like Spain, Argentina, and Peru, it seems that family ties are less important and that an education provides a significant factor in success. My question is: how do these factors affect each other?

I noticed that it is hard to name any clear trends across different countries, which goes to show how there is a diverse range of priorities among countries and even more diverse opinions of the 15-24-year-olds within these countries. Education does possess a noticeable general lead over the other factors in the graph, with a tendency for the less wealthy countries to value it moreso than the top few richest countries. 

I wonder how much the value placed upon education is correlated with its accessibility in that country, especially seeing the very high valuations the South American countries have placed upon it. I'm also very curious as to what some of the factors in the "other" category entail. A few of the leads in each of the categories have also caught my interest: Japan's high valuation of hard work vs. the lowest valuation of education (the work culture there?) and the U.S. valuing family wealth/connections the most.

This relates to myself and my community as the people around me and I are soon-to-be or newly fledged adults, and I think this is an age where we do consider what values and means are most important to us in helping us succeed in the future. 

How do we think success is created?

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: What’s Going On Inside The Minds of Young People?

I noticed that in most countries, approximately young people between 15-24 ages consider education and hard work as a priority for success, though not all completely. Peru seems to extremely consider education as a priority while Indonesia and Japan both seem to consider hard work as a priority. I also noticed that the U.S. considers education slightly less than hard work and wealth/connections. This makes me wonder, despite all the high quality and given the various education opportunities through top universities and colleges the U.S. is known for, why would young people consider it less? Would this decision differ depending on international students and U.S. students? Overall I noticed that education and hard work are the top 2 main factors young people consider for success. 
I wonder if this result has been like this continuously in past years or suddenly changed into this result recently. Would pre-pandemic, during, or after (possibly) differ the results hugely or little? I also wonder what made the people decide certain factors are more important than others for success, especially since the data is from young people, considering some people might still be in school, college, etc.
I think this information relates to my community and even to myself personally considering the ages mentioned and the results from the U.S. which I feel connected to as well.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph,  I notice that Argentina, Brazil, Peru, and India all strongly believe that education is an important factor in determining success. However, countries like the U.S., Japan, and the U.K. do not believe that education is a big determining factor in someone's success. Rather, they most believe that hard work is the most important. When it comes to family wealth or connections being a determining factor of one's success, the U.S. is a strong believer in this. Places like Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and India are not strong believers in family wealth or connections as a determining factor of one's success. I also noticed that the data collected from this graph was from 15- to 24-year-olds, which makes me wonder how people filtered out their views on what is the most important factor in determining one's success. I also wonder how other countries feel or if people from the countries on this graph do not agree with their own countries' response. This affects my community because my age group and country were represented in this graph. A catchy headline is "What Determine's The Success in One's Life."

I wonder if the different cultures of these countries contributed to these different beliefs. This relates to me and my community because as a senior in high school, many people are faced with the question of whether they feel that they should go to college to further their education. Whether or not someone decides to go to college, medical school, post-graduate school, etc. is reflective of how important they believe education is in success.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed that in the United States, hard work and family wealth/connections were considered to be the most important factors in determining success. Also, the U.S. has the largest percentage of young people that view family wealth/connections as a precursor to success. Hard work also seemed to be a factor most valued by young people in western individualist countries like the U.S., U.K., and France. I also noticed that education seemed to be valued most with regard to success in Peru, Brazil, Argentina, and India. I noticed that the young people residing in the wealthiest countries tended to value education the least as a factor of success, barring Germany, 
2. I wonder why education seems to be valued least as a factor in determining success in Japan, the U.S., and the U.K.. I also wonder how the data shown in the graph was collected and about the nature of the distribution of ages of the participants. comments.raw_comment:
The first thing that I noticed was that young Americans do not think education is the most important factor in determining success. To me, that was surprising because in my area of the US, education is considered the most important factor when it comes to achieving success. Large amounts of pressure is put on students for them to succeed academically. Additionally, it makes sense that Americans value hard work when it comes to success, because that is what the American dream is centered around. On the flip side, I also noticed that third world countries, such as Indonesia generally do not believe that family, wealth, or connections play a big part of success. 

I wonder how many 15-24 year olds responded to the question. I also wonder how many of them were of each age within that, because people who are 24 will most likely have a significantly different outlook compared to people who are 15 or 16. I also wonder why many countries in Africa and Asia place more value on hard work compared to countries in North America and Europe. Does it have to do with the economy, or just pure strength and determination? The last and probably most important question is, how do these individuals define success?

This graph affects me and my community because I am in the age group that was surveyed for this graph. I also think that people who grew up in various backgrounds will have a much different outlook than I have.

comments.raw_comment:
South American countries have high value in education, such as Argentina, Brazil, Peru. Asian countries such as Japan and Indonesia value hard work a lot. Zimbabwe is a statistical outlier compared to the rest of Africa when it comes to valuing hard work. Japan is a statistical outlier compared to other developed countries when it comes to valuing hard words. Bangladesh is another outlier compared to other undeveloped countries. 

Why does Cameroon value family wealth more than any other African? Why does Japan value hard work more than any other first-world country? Why is Japan the only wealthy/developed country that is still overworking itself to death? Do they have a toxic/harmful culture? What can "all, none or other" mean? And why do a lot of Bangladeshi people believe in it?

We should take examples from countries doing economically, socially, or maybe even socio-economically better than us and create ideas to improve our country, but NOT adopt the harmful aspects of it. Example: Japan's hard-working ethics has made them do miracles such as developing futuristic infrastructure, but they have a rampant problem with overworking themselves to death and high suicide. So we should adopt the Japanese work ethic but enough to kill ourselves. Their low interest in education most likely contributes to this problem as they wouldn't learn much about things such as mental health and thinking outside the box.

"How To Become Successful Around The World"

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that the different countries' values shift based on how they are structured such as their economies (capitalistic for example). Another factor that affects the results is the age range that they interviewed, younger people might focus more on education and its effects since they were in schooling more recently. Another way that being younger can affect the results is in the connections category, older generations had stronger connections and different values (more family-based) while younger generations have focused more on working for where they are. 

2. I wonder what are the different educations systems are like such as when the students start and end the education on average, what do the different countries consider "hard work", and why did the interviewers choose the countries that they did ( is it based on the different average incomes or some other factor?)?

3. I think that younger people will compare their values and the values of other countries and consider changing systems in place around them to fit the countries that excel the best to them. For example, if someone in the U.S sees that Peru focuses more on education than them and have a higher rate of people going on to have successful careers the person in the U.S might set up systems for those around them and future generations to have better education systems so that the community could improve and more people could succeed.

4. The Worlds Youths Outlook On Success.

comments.raw_comment:
From this graph, I can infer that young citizens in Peru seems to value education the most, and family wealth the least. Young Indonesians value Hard work the most, despite a lack of value in all of them together, and adolescents and young adults of The United States value Hard Work the most, just over Family Wealth and Education. The Younger population of Bangladesh seems to believe in all the most.
I wonder how much these opinions of the younger generations of each country are influenced by the countries themselves; whether it lies in their predominant cultures, religions, overlying economic system, education itself, or even geography.
This information allows for me and other people of the same generation to have insight into a general opinion on success, both in our country and other countries of our concern. Depending on heritage, or countries of origin or concern in another way, knowing the overlying opinions of each country on what young people believe is most important for success, can shed light on the cultural, educational, and labor-concerned beliefs of the same generation.
If I could create the headline; "Reaching For The Future; With What Today Holds Close"

In this graph, it depicts the percentage of what young people in each country thinks determines a successful life. The factors were education, hard work, family income/connections and a fourth option for all or none of the above. The numbers vary grately. India for example, had over 50% say it related to education while only 25% said it had to do with how hard you worked. Opposite in Kenya, where a little over 25% said education was the most important while close to 50% related it to hard work. I wonder what causes them to believe this and how much it relates to the culture of the country. Being from the United States, many of these stats make sense as hard work is often preached to be more important than an education from a prestigious university. 
"Growing Success for the Growing Generation"

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph relates how youth from various countries differ regarding which factors determine their success.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, March 11 with moderation on Wednesday, March 16.  The topic – extreme temperatures!  Keep noticing and wondering.

I notice how a countries social and economic circumstances influence the opinions of their youths. Lesser developed countries generally have a higher emphasis on education while having lower importance on family wealth and connections. Furthermore, hard work is a staple across all countries, especially so in certain places like Indonesia and Zimbabwe.

I wonder if a pattern could be made when one looks at countries grouped together. For example, South American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Peru) have a large emphasis on education. I wonder if this is the case with South America in general. Furthermore, can groups of nearby countries share the same sentiments about success?

Where I live in the US, our school education system is often looked down upon by the students themselves. Many talk about how the system needs improvement, whether it be more teachers, more life-applicable lessons, etc. On the other hand, a few peers talk about the importance of connections, whether it's schoolwork or life endeavors. In addition, hard work is universally treasured. As such, I especially agree with what the graph says about the US.

- What do you notice?
I notice that the 15-24-year old groups from a wide variety of countries carry an array of opinions on what the most important factor in determining success is, but for the most part, education and hard work are generally prioritized over family wealth or connections to people in this age range in most countries on this graph. 

- What do you wonder?
I wonder how they acquired this information, and why the people in this study believe that they have said.

- How does this relate to you and your community?
I think it relates to my community because many Americans in my age range believe that having connections or family wealth plays a major role in achieving success. However, many Americans also believe that hard work plays a big role. Many people in my community most likely believe either one of these would determine one's success in life.

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

        I personally noticed that in the United States, less than 25% of people from 15 to 24-years-old believed that education is important and rather believed that hard work and family wealth/connections was the most important factor in determining success. This is interesting considering that it is only the younger generation who is responding with their thoughts, which is ironically the part of the population which is in high school/college. 

2. What do you wonder?
 
       I wonder what countries such as Bangladesh had to say for "other" factors in determining success and why it may have been all or none. I also wonder why so much of the younger generation in Indonesia choose hard work over education, yet in Peru the younger generation chooses education over hard work. They are also relatively close in the sorting of wealth.

3. How does this relate to you and your community?

       This relates to my community and I since it shows what the younger generation in the United States think and how they think being born into wealth is the key to success rather than education or hard work. It shows a sense of realism yet simultaneously low hopes for the education system doing anything substantial for our success. 

4. What's going on in this graph?

       In this graph, we see the thoughts of the youth on which universal factors (though not equal in quality) determine success.

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

I notice that when countries have larger percents in one category that their percents for the other two are fairly low in comparison, for example Germany values Education for about 50% where the three other categories are all below 25%. In some cases all four categories are similar lengths like the France whose numbers are fairly equal but with a small decrease in family wealth or connections. it is interesting to see that those who value familial connections and wealth more equate to less priority of education or hard work in what makes success.

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder how they gathered this data, and if how their families and countries wealth was calculated into their response. I wonder what the All, none, or other categories mean and what the other categories that are factors of success are. 

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

I think that this says alot about the value systems of a country and what they equate success with. The US equates money and family wealth rather than more important things like education and hard work. 

4. Title:

What do younger generations equate success with: Education, Hard Work, or Old money?

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
What I first noticed upon looking at the graph was that, of the countries listed, most believe education and hard work are the greatest factors in determining success. I also noticed that this judgment is coming from a young audience who could be said to not have achieved success yet. An idea of where a country's values are can also be shown from this graph. 

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what were other variables that were believed to be a factor in determining success. Nigeria especially seems to be well divided among all the factors, and so It makes me wonder what other factors about 25% of people in Nigeria think determines success. Lastly, I want to know what their idea of success is. A lot of people can have different opinions on that and so it can affect the choices they make. 

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This is relevant to me and my community because I live in a well-diverse community and so this graph helps me grasp an idea of what most people with different backgrounds believe and where their values are. This can also potentially start a conversation where we can discover why people choose certain factors for determining success.

4. What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

What we can collect from this graph is how people of a younger generation believe success can be achieved. 

Catchy headline: What Path Do You Think LeadsTo Succes?

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

What I first noticed upon looking at the graph was that most countries believe education and hard work are the greatest factors in determining success. I also noticed that the opinions come from a young group who could be said to not have achieved success yet. An idea of where a country's values are can also be shown from this graph.
2. What do you wonder?

I wonder what were other variables that were believed to be a factor in determining success. Nigeria especially seems to be well divided among all the factors, and so It makes me wonder what other factors about 25% of people in Nigeria think determines success. Lastly, I want to know what their idea of success is. A lot of people can have different opinions on that and so it can affect the choices they make. 

3. How does this relate to you and your community?

This is relevant to me and my community because I live in a well-diverse community and so this graph helps me grasp an idea of what most people with different backgrounds believe and where their values are. This can also potentially start a conversation where we can discover why people choose certain factors for determining success.

4. What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

What we can collect from this graph is how people of a younger generation believe success can be achieved. 

Catchy headline: What Path Do You Think LeadsTo Succes?

I notice that Indonesia believes hard work is the most important factor in determining success, while Peru believes education is the most important. The U.S seems to believe hard work is fairly important for success. Family wealth or connections only goes up to 25%, which may be because not that many people believe it is an important deciding factor in success.

I wonder if the ages of the sample (15-24) make the results biased because higher levels of education (i.e. college) would be an important goal most would want to achieve. I wonder if poorer countries that rated education as the most important, like India chose that because they want to leave their country for better opportunities. 

This impacts my community because it shows how different countries may view the path to success. For example, in the U.K they value family wealth or connections the most, which implies that your future and success is already planned for you based on the type of family you are born into. This may be based upon their history of having a monarchy government. Meanwhile, most other countries value education or hard work, which means they believe you can change your future and how successful you'll be.

What do you notice?
I notice that 15-24-year-olds from many different countries have different opinions on what the most important factor in determining success is, but that for the most part, education and hard work are generally more important than family wealth or connections to people in this age range in most countries on this graph. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder how they got this information and why somebody decided to figure out this information. I also wonder if the people who answered this question were being completely truthful about their answer or if they just put what they thought should be considered the best, or most acceptable answer. 

What impact do you think this has on you and your community?
I think that this impacts our community because it shows us how people our own ages think about these things and how Americans our age do not appreciate or think of school as important as other countries may. This can help us get an idea of how kids our age think about success and what they think achieves it.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the graph separates the responses by country and answer. I also notice that the percentage of each answer for each country is shown at the bottom of the graph. As for the data itself, the answers are mostly distributed based on the countries' economic status. Most young people in the first world countries' answers had a higher percentage of "Family wealth or connections" and "Education", while most young people in second/third world countries' answers had higher percentages of "Hard work" and "Education."

I wonder: How does the economic status of a country effect young people's opinions on success? Compared to the US, where I live, what do other societies around the world teach their children about success? If the same survey was conducted and given to only adults, would the answers differ?

This graph gives a lot of insight into my community's view of success. According to the graph, the US determines wealth mostly on family wealth or connections and hard work. This is unexpected, especially because the American education system puts so much pressure on young people to do well in school. Without a good education in America, it's difficult to get a good job and become successful. This is a known fact. This graph, however, impacts our community by showing what young people actually think in opposition to the American education system.
